title: AS91946: Interpret and Apply Mathematical and Statistical Information
text:
1 Welcome
This guide combines the learning for both AS 1.1 (91944: Explore data using a statistical enquiry process) and AS 1.3 (91946: Interpret and apply statistical information). By highlighting where these two standards overlap, this resource eliminates unnecessary duplication and shows you how core statistical thinking connects the data you collect with the data you evaluate in everyday life.

title: AS91946: Interpret and Apply Mathematical and Statistical Information
text:
1.1 One toolkit, two assessments
You are not learning two separate subjects. The same toolkit appears in both courses:

AS1.1 (Internal) - statistical investigation in context
AS1.3 (External / 91946) - interpret and apply statistical information in context

In the internal assessment, you use that toolkit to plan an investigation, collect data, analyse it, and write a conclusion. In the external assessment, you use the same ideas to read graphs, interpret tables, question claims, and justify your reasoning under exam conditions.

title: 3  What is Statistics?
text:
3.1 Why statistics matters
Every day we are surrounded by data. News headlines cite poll results, sports commentators compare player averages, health campaigns report risk percentages, and social media shows us trending topics. Statistics is the science that helps us make sense of all this information.
At school, statistics helps you ask better questions, decide what evidence is relevant, and explain what the data does or does not support. Outside school, it helps you read media claims critically instead of accepting every graph or headline at face value.

title: 3  What is Statistics?
text:
NoteKey definition



Statistics is the practice of collecting, organising, summarising, analysing, and interpreting data in order to draw conclusions and make decisions.

title: 3  What is Statistics?
text:
3.2 Statistical questions and variability
Not all questions are statistical questions. A statistical question expects variability in the answers.






Tip



Statistical question: “How tall are the students in Year 11?”
(Heights will vary - this is statistical.)
Not a statistical question: “How tall is Ms Smith?”
(Only one answer - not statistical.)



3.2.1 Practice identifying statistical questions
Which of the following are statistical questions?

How many pages are in Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone?
How many hours per week do Year 11 students spend on homework?
What is the population of New Zealand?
What are the most popular music genres among teenagers in Auckland?
What colour is the school uniform?
How long does it take students in our class to get to school?
Which lunch option is chosen most often in the canteen each Friday?
How many goals did the first XI football team score this season?
What is the average screen time for Year 11 students on a school night?
How many desks are in Room 12?







NoteAnswer key






Not statistical - there is one fixed answer.
Statistical - different students spend different amounts of time.
Not statistical - there is one (changing but definite) answer.
Statistical - different teenagers have different preferences.
Not statistical - the uniform colour is fixed.
Statistical - travel times will vary between students.
Statistical - different students make different choices.
Not statistical - the season total is one fixed value.
Statistical - students will report different screen times.
Not statistical - there is one fixed count for that room.






3.2.2 A template for writing your own statistical question
Use this sentence frame when you are stuck:

What is the distribution of [variable] for [population] in [context]?

For example:

What is the distribution of weekly study time for Year 11 students at our school?
How does travel time to school differ for students who take the bus compared with students who walk?

title: 3  What is Statistics?
text:
3.3 Population, sample, and variable
These three ideas appear constantly in both the internal and the external.








Idea
What it means
School-based example




Population
The full group you want to know about
All Year 11 students at the school


Sample
The smaller group you actually collect data from
The 30 Year 11 students surveyed in form time


Variable
What you measure or record
Height, travel time, or favourite sport









WarningCommon trap



A large sample is not automatically a good sample. If the sample is biased, the conclusion can still be misleading.

title: 3  What is Statistics?
text:
3.4 Why context matters
In AS91946, context is central. You will always work with data that relates to real situations. When interpreting statistics, you must:

Name the variable being measured
State the units (e.g. centimetres, dollars, minutes)
Refer to the population the data came from
Relate findings back to the real-world situation

The strongest answers do more than quote a number. They explain what that number means for the people, objects, or events being studied.






WarningCommon mistake



Saying “the mean is 24” is not enough. Say
“The mean age of survey respondents was 24 years.”



3.4.1 Population vs sample in context
Suppose a school wants to know how much sleep Year 11 students get on a normal school night.

The population is all Year 11 students at the school.
A sample might be one statistics class or 40 students chosen at random.
The variable is hours of sleep on a school night.

If the sample only comes from one extension class, the results might not represent the whole year level. That is why context and sampling always matter when you interpret a summary or graph.

title: 3  What is Statistics?
text:
3.6 Exit ticket

Give two examples of statistical questions you could investigate at your school.
A student says “the average score is 65”. What is missing from this statement?
What is the difference between a population and a sample?
Write one sentence that uses a summary statistic in full context.
Explain why a sample could be large but still poor quality.







NoteExit ticket answers






Any valid examples should expect variation, such as study time, travel time, or sleep.
The variable, the units, and the group being described are missing.
The population is the whole group of interest; the sample is the smaller group actually measured.
Example: “The median travel time for Year 11 students in our survey was 18 minutes.”
A large sample can still be biased if it leaves out important groups or is collected unfairly.

title: 4  The Statistical Enquiry Cycle (PPDAC)
text:
4.1 Stage-by-stage guidance
New Zealand’s statistics curriculum uses the PPDAC cycle as the framework for carrying out statistical investigations and interpreting statistical information.

title: 4  The Statistical Enquiry Cycle (PPDAC)
text:
4.1.1 Problem
Write a statistical question that expects variability and identifies a clear context, variable, and population.


4.1.2 Plan
Decide how data will be collected, how the sample will be selected, and how fairness and bias will be managed.


4.1.3 Data
Collect and record the data accurately, with units and labels that can be interpreted later.


4.1.4 Analysis
Use graphs and summary statistics to identify patterns, centre, spread, and interesting features.


4.1.5 Conclusion
Answer the original question in context, using evidence from the analysis and acknowledging any limitations.

title: 4  The Statistical Enquiry Cycle (PPDAC)
text:
4.2 Common PPDAC mistakes

Starting analysis before writing a clear statistical question.
Using a sample that is large but biased.
Reporting numbers without units or context.
Giving a conclusion that does not answer the original question.

title: 4  The Statistical Enquiry Cycle (PPDAC)
text:
4.3 Quick check

Which PPDAC stage is most closely linked to reducing sampling bias?
Which stage should include comparison language and evidence from graphs?
Why must the conclusion link back to the original question?







NoteAnswers






Plan.
Analysis (with final interpretation carried into Conclusion).
Because PPDAC is question-driven, so conclusions must directly answer the statistical problem in context.

title: 5  Types of Data and Variables
text:
5.1 Categorical vs numerical data
Understanding the type of data you have is the first step in choosing the right graph or summary statistic. The wrong choice can make data hard to understand — or even misleading.
Classification of data types.
crumbs: 5  Types of Data and Variables

title: 5  Types of Data and Variables
text:
5.2 Categorical data
Categorical (qualitative) data describes qualities or categories. The values are labels, not numbers.

5.2.1 Nominal data
Nominal data has no natural order. Categories are just names.
Examples: - Eye colour (brown, blue, green, grey) - Favourite sport (rugby, netball, football, basketball) - Type of transport to school (bus, car, walk, bike)


5.2.2 Ordinal data
Ordinal data has a natural order, but the gaps between categories are not equal.
Examples: - Survey ratings (strongly disagree → disagree → neutral → agree → strongly agree) - Year group (Year 9, Year 10, Year 11, Year 12, Year 13) - Clothing size (XS, S, M, L, XL)
crumbs: 5  Types of Data and Variables

title: 5  Types of Data and Variables
text:
5.3 Numerical data
Numerical (quantitative) data represents quantities that can be measured or counted.

5.3.1 Discrete data
Discrete data can only take specific, separate values (usually whole numbers from counting).
Examples: - Number of siblings - Number of text messages sent per day - Goals scored in a rugby match


5.3.2 Continuous data
Continuous data can take any value within a range (usually from measuring).
Examples: - Height (cm) - Weight (kg) - Time to complete a race (seconds) - Temperature (°C)

title: 6  Independent and Dependent Variables
text:
6.1 Core idea
Correctly identifying variables is essential in both AS1.1 and AS1.3. If you mix them up, your graph choice, your analysis, and your conclusion can all become unclear.
A quick check:

title: 6  Independent and Dependent Variables
text:
Independent variable: the variable used to form groups, or the explanatory variable.
Dependent variable: the measured outcome, or the response variable.



Ask: “What am I comparing or using to explain change?” -> independent.
Ask: “What value is being measured as the result?” -> dependent.







TipMemory trick




Independent = what I choose, change, or group by.
Dependent = the Data that depends on that choice.

title: 6  Independent and Dependent Variables
text:
6.4 Worked example 1: comparison context
Question:

Do students who travel by bus, car, or bike have different daily study time?


Independent variable: transport mode (bus, car, bike)
Dependent variable: daily study time (hours)

Why:

Transport mode forms the groups.
Study time is measured inside each group.

title: 6  Independent and Dependent Variables
text:
6.5 Worked example 2: relationship context
Question:

Is there a relationship between hours of study and maths score?


Independent variable: hours of study
Dependent variable: maths score

Why:

Study hours is the explanatory variable on the x-axis.
Score is the response measured on the y-axis.

title: 6  Independent and Dependent Variables
text:
6.6 Common mistakes to avoid

Choosing two dependent variables and no clear explanatory variable.
Treating labels (for example, class names) as if they were measured outcomes.
Writing a conclusion without naming both variables in context.
Putting variables on the wrong axes in scatter plots.

text:
6.7 PPDAC link

Problem: write a clear question naming both variables and the population.

Analysis: display data using the correct variable roles.
Conclusion: make a claim in context about the relationship or comparison.

title: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes
text:
7.1 Why spread matters
Spread describes how consistent or variable a data set is. Two groups can have similar centres (like medians) but very different spread.
When you compare groups, spread tells you whether outcomes are tightly clustered (consistency) or widely scattered (variability).
crumbs: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes

title: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes
text:
Smaller spread -> more consistent performance.
Larger spread -> less consistent performance.
crumbs: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes

title: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes
text:
7.2 Key terms



Term
Meaning




Minimum
Smallest value in the data set


Maximum
Largest value in the data set


Range
Maximum - Minimum


Median (\(Q_2\))
Middle value of ordered data


Lower quartile (\(Q_1\))
Middle of lower half


Upper quartile (\(Q_3\))
Middle of upper half


Interquartile range (IQR)
\(Q_3 - Q_1\), spread of middle 50%

title: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes
text:
7.3 Core formulas
\[\text{Range} = \text{Maximum} - \text{Minimum}\]
\[\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\]
crumbs: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes

title: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes
text:
7.4 Step-by-step method

Put data in ascending order.
Find minimum and maximum, then calculate range.
Find the median (\(Q_2\)).
Split data into lower and upper halves.
Find \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) from those halves.
Calculate IQR.
crumbs: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes

title: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes
section: 7.5 Worked example A (odd number of values)
text:
7.5 Worked example A (odd number of values)
Data: \([3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15]\)

Minimum = \(3\)
Maximum = \(15\)
Range = \(15 - 3 = 12\)
Median (\(Q_2\)) = \(8\)
Lower half: \([3, 5, 6]\) so \(Q_1 = 5\)
Upper half: \([10, 12, 15]\) so \(Q_3 = 12\)
IQR = \(12 - 5 = 7\)

title: 7  Measures of Spread Study Notes
text:
7.7 Outliers and robust measures
An outlier can inflate the range heavily. The IQR is usually more stable because it ignores the lowest 25% and highest 25% of values.
In example B, the value 42 increases the range a lot, but the IQR still reflects where the middle 50% of scores sit.






TipGood comparison language




“Group A has a smaller IQR, so it is more consistent.”
“Group B has a larger range, suggesting more variability overall.”
“Because of an outlier, the range may overstate spread compared with IQR.”

title: 8  Statistical Graphs and Displays
text:
8.1 Setting up our data
A well-chosen graph makes patterns in data immediately visible. In this chapter you will learn to create, read, and critically interpret the most common statistical displays.
Before this chapter, make sure you are confident with Chapter 5, Chapter 6, and Chapter 7 so your graph choices and interpretations are statistically valid.
Throughout this chapter we use a simulated survey of 60 Year 11 students across a New Zealand school. The data includes variables on transport, height, study time, and maths scores.
Show R code
set.seed(2024)
n <- 60

students <- data.frame(
  transport  = sample(c("Bus", "Car", "Walk", "Bike"), n,
                      replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.25, 0.25, 0.1)),
  height_cm  = round(rnorm(n, mean = 167, sd = 9), 1),
  study_hrs  = round(pmax(0, rnorm(n, mean = 2.5, sd = 1.2)), 1),
  maths_score = round(pmin(100, pmax(0, rnorm(n, mean = 65, sd = 15))))
)

title: 8  Statistical Graphs and Displays
text:
8.2 Bar charts
Bar charts display the frequency (count) or relative frequency (proportion) of categorical data.


Show R code
transport_counts <- table(students$transport)

barplot(
  sort(transport_counts, decreasing = TRUE),
  col  = c("#4dac26", "#b8e186", "#f1b6da", "#d7191c"),
  main = "How Year 11 Students Travel to School",
  xlab = "Mode of Transport",
  ylab = "Number of Students",
  border = "white",
  las = 1
)








Figure 8.1: Bar chart showing how Year 11 students travel to school.






8.2.1 Reading a bar chart






Tip



When describing a bar chart, always comment on:

The most and least common categories
The overall pattern (are categories roughly equal, or is one dominant?)
The context — what does this tell us about the group?



Sample answer: “Bus is the most common way students travel to school, with over 20 students using this method. Bike is the least common. More students use public or active transport (bus, walk, bike) than passive transport (car).”

title: 8  Statistical Graphs and Displays
text:
8.3 Dot plots
Dot plots are useful for small numerical datasets. Each data point is shown as a dot above a number line.


Show R code
# Rounded to nearest 0.5 for clearer dot plot
study_rounded <- round(students$study_hrs * 2) / 2

stripchart(
  study_rounded,
  method = "stack",
  pch    = 19,
  col    = "#0571b0",
  cex    = 1.4,
  xlab   = "Daily Study Hours",
  main   = "Daily Study Hours — Year 11 Students",
  offset = 0.4
)








Figure 8.2: Dot plot of daily study hours for Year 11 students.

title: 8  Statistical Graphs and Displays
text:
8.4 Histograms
A histogram shows the distribution of continuous numerical data by grouping values into intervals (bins).


Show R code
hist(
  students$height_cm,
  breaks = 10,
  col    = "#2c7bb6",
  border = "white",
  main   = "Distribution of Student Heights",
  xlab   = "Height (cm)",
  ylab   = "Frequency",
  las    = 1
)








Figure 8.3: Histogram of student heights (cm).






8.4.1 Describing a histogram — SOCS
Use SOCS to describe a distribution:







Letter
What to describe




Shape
Symmetric, skewed left, skewed right, uniform, bimodal


Outliers
Any unusual values far from the main group


Centre
Where the middle of the data is (mean or median)


Spread
How variable the data is (range, IQR, standard deviation)





Show R code
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

# Symmetric
set.seed(1)
hist(rnorm(500, 50, 10), breaks = 15, col = "#4dac26", border = "white",
     main = "Symmetric", xlab = "", ylab = "Frequency", las = 1)

# Right-skewed
hist(rexp(500, 0.1), breaks = 15, col = "#f4a582", border = "white",
     main = "Right (positive) skew", xlab = "", ylab = "", las = 1)

hist(100 - rexp(500, 0.1), breaks = 15, col = "#92c5de", border = "white",

8.7 Scatter plots
Scatter plots show the relationship between two numerical variables.


Show R code
plot(
  students$study_hrs, students$maths_score,
  pch  = 19,
  col  = adjustcolor("#0571b0", alpha.f = 0.7),

8.7.1 Describing a scatter plot
Comment on:

Direction — positive, negative, or no association
Form — linear or non-linear
Strength — strong, moderate, or weak
Outliers — any unusual points







WarningCorrelation ≠ Causation



Just because two variables are related does not mean one causes the other. Always think about whether an association makes sense in context.

title: 9  Bivariate Data in Ecology
text:
9.1 Exercise: Project Kōura
Investigating koura habitats using the PPDAC cycle
In this chapter, we apply the PPDAC (Problem, Plan, Data, Analysis, Conclusion) statistical enquiry cycle to a real-world ecological context. Understanding how two numerical variables interact is a core component of NCEA Level 1 Statistics.
Context: A group of students—Jack, Trishav, and Levi—are conducting a local ecological survey, which they have named “Project Kōura”. They are investigating the populations of native freshwater crayfish (kōura) across several local catchments, including the Kaikorai Stream and the Water of Leith. They want to know if the physical environment of the stream affects the growth of the kōura. They have accessed an open dataset from the New Zealand Freshwater Fish Database (NZFFD) containing recent survey results.

title: 9  Bivariate Data in Ecology
text:
9.1.1 1. Problem
Before looking at the data, the group needs to define a clear investigative question. Jack suggests they look at the relationship between the water temperature of the stream and the size of the kōura.
Task A: Write a suitable investigative question for this survey. Ensure you specify the variables, the population, and the direction of your investigation.
Task B: Write a hypothesis. Based on what you know about freshwater biology, what kind of relationship do you expect to see between water temperature and kōura carapace length?


9.1.2 2. Plan
The students isolate two numerical variables from the NZFFD dataset:

Explanatory Variable: Stream Temperature (°C)
Response Variable: Carapace Length (mm)

Task C: Why is Stream Temperature the explanatory variable and Carapace Length the response variable, rather than the other way around?


9.1.3 3. Data
We will simulate importing the NZFFD dataset directly into R to prepare it for analysis.


Show R code
# Load necessary libraries
library(tidyverse)

# Simulate importing the NZFFD dataset

  temp_c = runif(100, 8, 16),
  # Simulating a negative correlation: cooler water tends to support larger kōura
  carapace_length_mm = 60 - (1.5 * temp_c) + rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 4) 
)

title: 10  Measures of Centre and Spread
text:
10.1 Measures of centre
Once you have a graph, you need numerical summaries to describe and compare distributions precisely. The two key things to describe are:
crumbs: 10  Measures of Centre and Spread

title: 10  Measures of Centre and Spread
text:
10.1.1 The mean
The mean (average) is calculated by adding all values and dividing by the number of values:
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]


Show R code
set.seed(2024)
scores <- c(55, 62, 68, 70, 72, 75, 78, 80, 83, 85,
            88, 60, 91, 74, 66, 79, 52, 95, 73, 71)
n <- length(scores)

cat("Scores:", sort(scores), "\n")
#> Scores: 52 55 60 62 66 68 70 71 72 73 74 75 78 79 80 83 85 88 91 95
cat("Mean:  ", round(mean(scores), 2), "\n")
#> Mean:   73.85
cat("n =    ", n, "\n")
#> n =     20




10.1.2 The median
The median is the middle value when data is sorted from smallest to largest. It is not affected by outliers.

If n is odd: median = middle value
If n is even: median = average of the two middle values



Show R code
sorted_scores <- sort(scores)
cat("Sorted scores:\n", sorted_scores, "\n\n")
#> Sorted scores:
#>  52 55 60 62 66 68 70 71 72 73 74 75 78 79 80 83 85 88 91 95
cat("n = 20 (even) → median = mean of 10th and 11th values\n")
#> n = 20 (even) → median = mean of 10th and 11th values
cat("10th value:", sorted_scores[10], "\n")
#> 10th value: 73
cat("11th value:", sorted_scores[11], "\n")
#> 11th value: 74
cat("Median =", median(scores), "\n")
#> Median = 73.5




10.1.3 The mode
The mode is the most frequently occurring value. Data can have: - No mode (all values appear once) - One mode (unimodal) - Two modes (bimodal) - More than two modes (multimodal)


Show R code
# Custom mode function (base R has no built-in mode for numeric)
stat_mode <- function(x) {
  tbl <- table(x)
  as.numeric(names(tbl)[tbl == max(tbl)])
}

test_data <- c(4, 7, 2, 7, 9, 7, 3, 4, 5, 4)
cat("Data:", test_data, "\n")
#> Data: 4 7 2 7 9 7 3 4 5 4
cat("Mode(s):", stat_mode(test_data), "\n")
#> Mode(s): 4 7




10.1.4 When to use each measure of centre



Measure
Best used when…
Affected by outliers?




Mean
Data is roughly symmetric, no outliers
Yes


Median
Data is skewed or has outliers
No


Mode
Data is categorical; or finding most common value
No





Show R code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Without outlier
x1 <- c(10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20)
hist(x1, col = "#4dac26", border = "white", main = "No Outlier",
     xlab = "Value", ylab = "Frequency", xlim = c(0, 80), breaks = 5)
abline(v = mean(x1),   col = "#d7191c", lwd = 2, lty = 1)
abline(v = median(x1), col = "#0571b0", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c(paste("Mean =", mean(x1)),
                     paste("Median =", median(x1))),
       col = c("#d7191c", "#0571b0"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")

# With outlier
x2 <- c(x1, 75)
hist(x2, col = "#f4a582", border = "white", main = "With Outlier (75)",
     xlab = "Value", ylab = "", xlim = c(0, 80), breaks = 8)
abline(v = mean(x2),   col = "#d7191c", lwd = 2, lty = 1)
abline(v = median(x2), col = "#0571b0", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c(paste("Mean =", round(mean(x2), 1)),
                     paste("Median =", median(x2))),
       col = c("#d7191c", "#0571b0"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 10.1: Effect of outliers on mean vs median.
crumbs: 10  Measures of Centre and Spread

title: 10  Measures of Centre and Spread
text:
10.2 Measures of spread

10.2.1 Range
The range is the simplest measure of spread:
\[\text{Range} = \text{Maximum} - \text{Minimum}\]


Show R code
cat("Range of scores:", max(scores) - min(scores), "\n")
#> Range of scores: 43
cat("  (Max =", max(scores), ", Min =", min(scores), ")\n")
#>   (Max = 95 , Min = 52 )




10.2.2 Quartiles and the interquartile range (IQR)
Quartiles divide sorted data into four equal groups:



Quartile
Description




Q1 (lower quartile)
25% of data falls below this value


Q2 (median)
50% of data falls below this value


Q3 (upper quartile)
75% of data falls below this value



The interquartile range (IQR) is the spread of the middle 50% of data:
\[\text{IQR} = Q3 - Q1\]


Show R code
q <- quantile(scores)
cat("Five-number summary:\n")
#> Five-number summary:
cat("  Minimum:", q[1], "\n")
#>   Minimum: 52
cat("  Q1:     ", q[2], "\n")
#>   Q1:      67.5
cat("  Median: ", q[3], "\n")
#>   Median:  73.5
cat("  Q3:     ", q[4], "\n")
#>   Q3:      80.75
cat("  Maximum:", q[5], "\n")
#>   Maximum: 95
cat("  IQR =", q[4] - q[2], "\n")
#>   IQR = 13.25




10.2.3 Standard deviation
The standard deviation measures how spread out data values are from the mean. A larger standard deviation means more variability.
\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}\]


Show R code
cat("Mean:", round(mean(scores), 2), "\n")
#> Mean: 73.85
cat("Standard deviation:", round(sd(scores), 2), "\n")
#> Standard deviation: 11.52








TipRule of thumb



For roughly symmetric distributions, about 68% of data falls within one standard deviation of the mean, and 95% falls within two standard deviations (the empirical rule / 68-95-99.7 rule).




10.2.4 Choosing the right measure of spread








Measure
Use with…
Advantage




Range
Quick overview
Easy to calculate


IQR
Skewed data or when outliers present
Resistant to outliers


Standard deviation
Symmetric data, no outliers
Uses all data values

title: 10  Measures of Centre and Spread
text:
10.4 Identifying outliers
A value is often flagged as an outlier if it falls more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3:
\[\text{Lower fence} = Q1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\] \[\text{Upper fence} = Q3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\]


Show R code
Q1  <- quantile(scores, 0.25)
Q3  <- quantile(scores, 0.75)
iqr <- Q3 - Q1

lower_fence <- Q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_fence <- Q3 + 1.5 * iqr

cat("Q1 =", Q1, "\n")
#> Q1 = 67.5
cat("Q3 =", Q3, "\n")
#> Q3 = 80.75
cat("IQR =", iqr, "\n")
#> IQR = 13.25
cat("Lower fence:", lower_fence, "\n")
#> Lower fence: 47.625
cat("Upper fence:", upper_fence, "\n")
#> Upper fence: 100.625
cat("Outliers:", scores[scores < lower_fence | scores > upper_fence], "\n")
#> Outliers:

title: 10  Measures of Centre and Spread
text:
10.6 Check your understanding
Use the dataset: 12, 15, 18, 18, 20, 22, 25, 25, 28, 100

Calculate the mean and median. Which is more appropriate as a measure of centre for this data? Why?
Find Q1, Q3, and the IQR.
Calculate the range.
Is 100 an outlier? Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to justify your answer.
Sketch a box plot of this data.







NoteAnswers






Mean = (12+15+18+18+20+22+25+25+28+100)/10 = 283/10 = 28.3; Median = (20+22)/2 = 21. The median is more appropriate because of the outlier (100) which pulls the mean up.
Q1 = 18, Q3 = 25, IQR = 7.
Range = 100 − 12 = 88.
Upper fence = 25 + 1.5 × 7 = 25 + 10.5 = 35.5. Since 100 > 35.5, yes, 100 is an outlier.
Sketch: whiskers from 12 to 35.5, box from 18 to 25, median line at 21, and a dot at 100 representing the outlier.

The council used a telephone survey conducted at 2 pm on weekdays. Identify one source of bias and explain how it might affect the results.
Can we conclude from this data that teenagers exercise more because they are younger? Explain.







NoteModel answers





1. Centre: The median exercise hours for teenagers (approx. 7.1 hrs) is higher than for adults (4.35 hrs). This suggests teenagers in this sample tend to do more weekly exercise than adults.
2. Spread: The IQR and standard deviation are larger for teenagers (3.6 hrs vs 2.9 hrs). This means teenagers’ exercise habits are more variable — some exercise a lot while others exercise very little. Adults’ exercise habits are more consistent.
3. Bias: Calling at 2 pm on weekdays means working adults are unlikely to answer (they are at work). This leads to non-response bias — the adult sample may over-represent retired or part-time workers, who may exercise more than the general adult population.
4. Causation: No — we cannot conclude that age causes the difference in exercise. Teenagers may exercise more because they participate in school sport, not because of their age per se. Age and exercise are correlated in this sample, but there may be confounding variables such as school PE requirements, free time, or lifestyle factors.

11.6 Practice set 3 — Excellence level
A researcher claims: “A study of 50 Auckland households found that households with more bookshelves have higher household income. Therefore, buying more bookshelves will increase your income.”
Questions:

Identify the two variables and their types.
Explain why this conclusion is flawed. Use statistical language.
Suggest one confounding variable that could explain the relationship.
What would the researcher need to do to properly establish causation?
The sample was 50 Auckland households selected by going door-to-door in Remuera (a wealthy suburb). Evaluate the reliability of generalising these findings to all New Zealand households.







NoteModel answers





1. Number of bookshelves: numerical, discrete. Household income: numerical, continuous.
2. The conclusion confuses correlation with causation. Even if the two variables are positively correlated, this does not mean bookshelves cause higher income. The relationship could be due to a third variable, and correlation studies cannot establish cause-and-effect without experimental control.
3. Wealth/education level — wealthier, more educated households are more likely to own books/bookshelves AND to have higher income. Both variables are driven by a common factor.
4. To establish causation, the researcher would need a controlled experiment — randomly assigning households to receive bookshelves or not, holding all other variables constant, and measuring income change over time. This would be impractical.
5. The sample has significant sampling bias. Remuera is one of Auckland’s wealthiest suburbs. The sample does not represent the diversity of New Zealand households in terms of income, region, or ethnicity. Results cannot be reliably generalised to all New Zealand households. A stratified random sample from across New Zealand would be needed.

title: 12  Probability
text:
12.1 Probability scale
Probability is a measure of how likely an event is to occur. It is expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), or as a percentage.
\[P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}}\]
Figure 12.1: The probability scale from impossible (0) to certain (1).

title: 12  Probability
text:
12.2 Key vocabulary



Term
Definition




Experiment
A process with uncertain outcomes


Outcome
A single possible result


Event
One or more outcomes grouped together


Sample space
The set of all possible outcomes


Complementary event
All outcomes that are NOT in the event

title: 12  Probability
text:
12.3 Simple probability — equally likely outcomes
When all outcomes are equally likely, we can use the classical definition.

12.3.1 Example: rolling a die


Show R code
sample_space <- 1:6
cat("Sample space:", sample_space, "\n")
#> Sample space: 1 2 3 4 5 6

# P(rolling a 4)
p_four <- sum(sample_space == 4) / length(sample_space)
cat("P(rolling a 4) =", p_four, "\n")
#> P(rolling a 4) = 0.1666667

# P(rolling an even number)
p_even <- sum(sample_space %% 2 == 0) / length(sample_space)
cat("P(even number) =", p_even, "\n")
#> P(even number) = 0.5

# P(rolling > 4)
p_gt4 <- sum(sample_space > 4) / length(sample_space)
cat("P(> 4) =", p_gt4, "\n")
#> P(> 4) = 0.3333333

title: 12  Probability
text:
12.4 Complementary events
The complement of event A (written A’ or \(\bar{A}\)) contains all outcomes NOT in A.
\[P(A') = 1 - P(A)\]
Example: If the probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3, then:
\[P(\text{no rain}) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7\]


Show R code
p_rain <- 0.3
p_no_rain <- 1 - p_rain
cat("P(rain) =", p_rain, "\n")
#> P(rain) = 0.3
cat("P(no rain) = 1 -", p_rain, "=", p_no_rain, "\n")
#> P(no rain) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7

title: 12  Probability
text:
12.5 Experimental (relative frequency) probability
When we cannot calculate probability theoretically, we estimate it by repeating an experiment many times:
\[P(\text{event}) \approx \frac{\text{number of times event occurred}}{\text{total number of trials}}\]

12.5.1 Simulating coin flips


Show R code
set.seed(99)
flips  <- sample(c("Heads", "Tails"), 1000, replace = TRUE)
cumulative_heads <- cumsum(flips == "Heads") / seq_along(flips)

plot(
  cumulative_heads,
  type = "l",
  col  = "#0571b0",
  lwd  = 1.5,
  xlab = "Number of Flips",
  ylab = "Relative Frequency of Heads",
  main = "Simulated Coin Flips",
  ylim = c(0, 1),
  las  = 1
)
abline(h = 0.5, col = "#d7191c", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Relative frequency", "True probability (0.5)"),
       col = c("#0571b0", "#d7191c"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")








Figure 12.2: Relative frequency of heads approaches 0.5 as the number of flips increases (the law of large numbers).











NoteLaw of Large Numbers



As the number of trials increases, the relative frequency (experimental probability) gets closer and closer to the true probability. This is why surveys and experiments need large samples.

12.6 Two-way tables
A two-way table (contingency table) organises data by two categorical variables and is very useful for calculating probabilities.

Using the table above:

    round(sum(tbl[, "Male"]) / total, 3), "\n")

title: 12  Probability
text:
12.7 Tree diagrams
Tree diagrams help calculate probabilities for sequential events.








Figure 12.3: Tree diagram for drawing two balls from a bag (with replacement).





Key rule: Multiply probabilities along each branch, add probabilities for different paths leading to the same outcome.

title: 12  Probability
text:
12.8 Expected value (extension)
For a simple scenario, the expected value is the long-run average outcome:
\[E(X) = \sum x \cdot P(x)\]
Example: A raffle has 200 tickets at $2 each. First prize is $100, second prize is $50. What is the expected gain per ticket?


Show R code
outcomes  <- c(100, 50, 0)         # winnings
probs     <- c(1/200, 1/200, 198/200)
cost      <- 2

expected_win  <- sum(outcomes * probs)
expected_gain <- expected_win - cost

cat("Expected winnings:", expected_win, "\n")
#> Expected winnings: 0.75
cat("Ticket cost:      ", cost, "\n")
#> Ticket cost:       2
cat("Expected net gain:", expected_gain, "\n")
#> Expected net gain: -1.25
cat("(A negative expected gain means this is not a good investment!)\n")
#> (A negative expected gain means this is not a good investment!)

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.1 Reading statistical claims
A major focus of AS91946 is the ability to critically read and interpret statistical information from a variety of sources — including newspapers, websites, government reports, and scientific studies.
Statistical claims appear everywhere in everyday life. As a critical consumer of information, you need to ask:

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
Who collected the data and why?
How was the data collected (survey, experiment, census)?
How many people or things were measured (sample size)?
Who was sampled — does the sample represent the population?
What do the numbers actually mean in context?

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.2 Sources of bias
Bias is a systematic error that causes results to be unrepresentative.








Type of bias
Description
Example




Sampling bias
Sample does not represent population
Surveying only Year 11s about a school-wide issue


Response bias
People don’t answer truthfully
“Do you cheat on tests?”


Non-response bias
Certain groups are less likely to respond
Online survey misses those without internet


Leading question bias
Question wording influences the answer
“Don’t you agree that homework is too much?”


Volunteer bias
Only motivated people respond
Self-selected online polls











Figure 13.1: Different types of bias and how they affect results.

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.3 Sample size and reliability
Larger samples generally give more reliable results — but size alone is not enough if the sample is biased.


Show R code
set.seed(42)
true_prop <- 0.55  # True proportion in population
sample_sizes <- c(10, 30, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)
n_simulations <- 1000

set.seed(321)
variability <- sapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  estimates <- replicate(n_simulations, mean(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), n,
                                                    replace = TRUE,
                                                    prob = c(true_prop,
                                                             1 - true_prop))))
  sd(estimates)
})

plot(
  sample_sizes, variability,
  type = "b",
  pch  = 19,
  col  = "#0571b0",
  lwd  = 2,
  xlab = "Sample Size (n)",
  ylab = "Standard Deviation of Estimates",
  main = "Sample Size vs Variability of Estimates",
  las  = 1
)
abline(h = 0, col = "#d7191c", lty = 2)








Figure 13.2: Variability in sample estimates decreases as sample size increases.

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.4 Correlation and causation
One of the most important concepts in statistical literacy is understanding the difference between correlation and causation.






WarningCorrelation ≠ Causation



Two variables can be correlated (move together) without one causing the other. There may be a confounding variable responsible for both.



13.4.1 Famous spurious correlations

Ice cream sales and shark attacks both increase in summer → they are both caused by hot weather, not each other.
Countries with more TVs have longer life expectancy → both are driven by wealth, not TVs causing people to live longer.









Figure 13.3: A spurious correlation: ice cream sales and drownings both increase in summer.

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.5 Interpreting graphs critically
When reading statistical graphs, watch out for:

13.5.1 Misleading y-axis
A y-axis that doesn’t start at zero can make small differences look huge.


Show R code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

years   <- 2020:2024
revenue <- c(980, 990, 995, 1005, 1010)

# Misleading
plot(years, revenue, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#d7191c", lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(975, 1015), xlab = "Year", ylab = "Revenue ($M)",
     main = "Misleading: Truncated Axis", las = 1)

# Honest
plot(years, revenue, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#4dac26", lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, 1100), xlab = "Year", ylab = "Revenue ($M)",
     main = "Honest: Starting at Zero", las = 1)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 13.4: The same data displayed with a truncated y-axis (left) vs starting at zero (right).







13.5.2 Percentage vs absolute numbers






TipBe careful with percentages



“Crime increased by 100%” sounds alarming — but if there were only 2 crimes last year and 4 this year, the absolute increase is tiny.
Always ask: 100% of what?




13.5.3 Averages without context
The mean can be pulled by extreme values, making it misleading if used alone. Always ask what measure of centre was used and whether it is appropriate.

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.6 Reading media reports — a framework
Use these questions when evaluating a statistical claim in the media:

What is being measured? (the variable and its units)
Who was studied? (the population and sample)
How was data collected? (method and potential biases)
How large was the sample?
What is the source? (government, independent researcher, company with a vested interest?)
Are conclusions supported by the evidence? Or is the claim overstated?
Are comparisons fair? Are groups being compared actually comparable?

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.7 A worked example






NoteNews headline



“Study shows eating chocolate improves exam scores by 15%”


Critical analysis:

What was measured? Exam scores before and after eating chocolate.
Who was studied? Not stated — red flag!
Sample size? Not given — could be only 10 students.
Confounding variables? Students who eat chocolate may be from wealthier families with better study resources.
Causation or correlation? This is a correlational study; chocolate doesn’t necessarily cause better scores.
Who funded it? If a chocolate company funded it, there is a conflict of interest.

Conclusion: The headline is likely exaggerated or misleading. We would need much more information before accepting this claim.

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.8 Glossary







Term
Definition




Bias
Systematic error that distorts results


Confounding variable
A hidden variable that explains an apparent relationship


Correlation
A statistical relationship between two variables


Causation
One variable directly causes a change in another


Reliable
Consistent results if repeated


Valid
Measuring what it claims to measure


Population
The full group of interest


Sample
A subset of the population

title: 13  Interpreting Statistical Information
text:
13.9 Check your understanding

A newspaper article claims: “People who eat breakfast earn more money than those who skip it.” Identify a possible confounding variable.
A survey found that 80% of students support a longer lunch break. The survey was conducted by standing outside the school canteen. What type of bias is this? How might it affect results?
A graph shows the number of electric vehicles sold in New Zealand, with the y-axis starting at 45,000 rather than 0. Sales increased from 47,000 to 51,000. On the graph, this looks like a 400% increase. Calculate the true percentage increase.
Explain the difference between correlation and causation using your own example.







NoteAnswers






Wealthier people are more likely to eat breakfast (they can afford food) and also earn more — wealth is the confounding variable.
Sampling bias / volunteer bias — students near the canteen are more likely to want a longer lunch break. Results will overestimate support.
True % increase = (51,000 − 47,000) / 47,000 × 100 ≈ 8.5%.
Accept any reasonable example, e.g., “Countries with more hospitals have higher death rates — hospitals don’t cause death; both are linked to population size.”
